title: Witnesses testify on first day of inquest; Man who died after being arrested seen screaming, breaking windows on 100th Street
article: Larry McPherson was running from his room at the Cedar Lodge screaming for help just minutes before he was tackled by police and arrested.

Those are the testimonies given by a security guard and a taxi driver, who saw him the night of Aug. 28, 2007, at a coroner's inquest into the man's death that began Wednesday in Fort St. John Supreme Court.
McPherson was pronounced dead at the Fort St. John Hospital after his arrest. According to an RCMP press release last year, he went into cardiac arrest after losing and regaining consciousness.

"I could hear screaming and yelling 'help, help.' And I heard a door slam," said Darwin Blacklock, who was a security guard at the Quality Inn Northern Grand when he said he saw McPherson run across 100th Avenue and pull on the locked doors of the hotel.
When Blacklock walked up to him to say the doors were locked, McPherson stared at him, then bolted towards 100th Street and turned south towards the Alaska Highway.

Taxi driver Gary Tait told the inquiry he followed McPherson south on 100th Street in his cab thinking he needed help, and then watched McPherson smash a squeegee into the window at the Shell gas station and throw rocks into the window of two other businesses, breaking one.
By the time McPherson reached the Stonebridge Hotel with a rock in one hand, police arrived on scene and ordered him to drop the rock.
McPherson complied, but turned to run towards the highway before being tackled and handcuffed by police officers, Tait said.
"It appeared to me they all jumped on top of him. It was like a football match almost," he said. "I heard him say 'I'm not resisting' several times."
Tait said the officers then tried to pull him into the car, but weren't able to, and held him on the ground to restrain him.

That's when Tait said McPherson began to shake uncontrollably, as though he were having a seizure, and officers covered him with a blanket and appeared to be examining him before the ambulance arrived.
It was at least 15 minutes before the ambulance left to take McPherson to the hospital, Tait said.

It wasn't the first time McPherson had been seen in such distress. Three days earlier he called police and fled from the Caravan Hotel, telling Const. Erin Davis several men had threatened him, according to her testimony.
"McPherson stated they were in the hotel watching the T.V. when two men burst into the room and threatened to kick his ass," she told the court.
The man McPherson was staying with was supposed to testify at the inquiry yesterday morning, but didn't attend. He is rescheduled to testify Thursday at 9 a.m. from Terrace.

Inquest council Mitch Houg, who represents the community in the inquiry into McPherson's death, said in his opening statement that McPherson had a history of drug use, including cocaine, and had just quit his job with plans to move to Terrace.

Houg repeatedly asked witnesses whether they noticed several scrapes on his face or an injured knee that were found in the autopsy, but no one could confirm they noticed any injuries prior to the arrest.

The goal of the inquiry is to determine facts surrounding the death, such as the cause, and provide recommendations to prevent similar deaths in the future. Coroner's inquests are mandatory for all deaths in police custody in B.C.
The one man and four women on the jury will be asked to classify the death as either natural, accidental, suicide, homicide or undetermined.
The regional coroner presiding over the case is Shane DeMeyer, and Andrew Kemp is representing the RCMP.
The police officers involved in the arrest are scheduled to speak Thursday, while the autopsy, toxicology and other medical reports will be presented Friday.

McPherson's sister, Lori McPherson, is scheduled to testify last. She sat in the front row next to her mother, Alberta McPherson, wearing a blue blouse and scribbling notes they passed to council to ask witnesses.
The family said they had been kept in the dark on much of the information, and this was their first chance to learn the truth about how McPherson died.
